before.exam_tip_html: When a question uses the command word ‘Describe’ for a priestess or festival, give at least three factual details: what the person or festival was, where it took place, and what specific role women played. The examiner rewards precise knowledge. When the question asks you to ‘Explain’ or ‘Analyse’ a source, resist simply narrating what it shows — push to say what it reveals about the status of women or the culture’s values. The most common error in essays on women and religion is over-generalising: students write “women had no power” when the evidence of the Vestals and the Pythia shows the opposite. Use named sources (Parthenon Frieze, the Vestal’s House, Plutarch) to support every claim.

When a source analysis question shows you a material source such as the Lion Gate, always describe it precisely first — what you can see, the material, the scale — before moving to interpretation. Examiners reward students who use specific details from the source rather than general background knowledge alone. For ‘Describe’ questions about Mycenae or Tiryns, name the specific features: the Lion Gate, the Cyclopean walls, Grave Circle A, the megaron. Avoid vague answers such as “it had big walls and a palace.”

For ‘Describe’ questions about the megaron, work through the layout systematically: porch, anteroom, main hall, central hearth, four columns, throne. Name the specific rooms in sequence rather than giving a vague general description. When using Homer as evidence for Mycenaean palace life, always note that the poems were composed centuries after the Bronze Age and may blend historical memory with poetic invention — examiners reward this kind of critical awareness. Over-narrating what happens in the Odyssey without connecting it to evidence is the most common error in this topic.

Questions about priests often ask you to Explain their role or to Compare Greek and Roman religious officials. The crucial point is that priests in both cultures were ritual specialists, not moral or spiritual guides. Examiners reward students who distinguish between the different roles: the Greek hiereus/hiereia who served a specific god at a specific temple; the Greek mantis who accompanied armies to read omens; the Roman pontifices who policed religious law; and the Roman augures who read the auspices. For source-analysis questions about the Pythia, use specific details in the source (the tripod, the vapours, the ambiguous phrasing of the oracle) and explain what they show about the Greeks’ belief in direct communication with the gods. Over-narrating the story of Croesus without making an analytical point is the most common mistake here.

When answering essay questions about Roman warfare and expansion, avoid simply listing battles and dates. The examiner wants you to argue — for example, arguing that engineering was more important than weapons, or that propaganda (Trajan’s Column, the Arch at Benevento) tells us as much about Roman values as about what actually happened. Use named sources as evidence for your argument, not just as decoration. Common pitfall: treating Trajan’s Column as a neutral record rather than as a monument designed to glorify the emperor.

When comparing Spartan and Athenian women in an essay, do not simply describe two systems separately. Examiners reward analytical comparison: identify a key point of difference (e.g. property ownership, physical freedom, marriage age), explain why each society organised things that way, and then make a judgement. For source analysis questions using Plutarch’s Sayings of Spartan Women or similar, remember to consider the source’s purpose and audience: Plutarch is writing centuries later and is celebrating Spartan virtues. Always ask: is this source telling us what really happened, or what the author wanted to be true?

For questions asking you to evaluate Odysseus as a hero, avoid simply listing his qualities. Examiners want to see you engage with the complexity: what are his strengths, what are his weaknesses, and how does Homer use specific episodes to reveal both? Always name the book and the episode (e.g. ‘in Book 9, his pride when he reveals his name to Polyphemus’). For essay questions that ask ‘how far do you agree,’ you must present both sides: the case that Odysseus is a great hero (metis, endurance, his relationships) and the case that his flaws undermine this (hubris, ruthlessness, the deaths of his crew). Reach a clear, supported conclusion — sitting on the fence is not a judgement.

For questions asking you to evaluate Pompeii and Herculaneum as evidence, the strongest answers weigh both the strengths (unique preservation, wide range of evidence, inscriptions capturing ordinary voices) and the limitations (frozen at AD 79, disrupted by the AD 62 earthquake, provincial Italian towns not Rome itself). Avoid treating “it was preserved by the volcano” as your only strength — examiners want to see that you understand what kinds of things were preserved and why they matter. Always name specific sites or finds: the Insula of Diana, the Forum Baths at Herculaneum, Pliny’s letters, the graffiti. Vague references to “Pompeii shows us...” without a specific example will not score highly.

The Underworld is rich in source material: the Homeric Hymn to Demeter and Ovid’s Metamorphoses 10.1–64 are both prescribed texts. For source analysis questions, make sure you can pick out specific details from the passage and link them to wider meaning. For the Hymn to Demeter, the key points are the nature of Demeter’s grief (she abandons her divine role, causing famine — shows how deeply the gods are tied to the natural world) and the compromise of the pomegranate (explains the seasons through a legal ruling in the Underworld). For Orpheus, the key point is the moment of looking back — explain both the literal failure (the condition was broken) and the deeper meaning (love cannot follow rules; the Underworld’s laws are absolute). Always avoid simply retelling the myth — examiners reward analysis of what the myth reveals about ancient beliefs.
